world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Only survey/subclassification sources (Clouse 1997; Voorhoeve 1975) on Glottolog; no grammar or phonology located.

new_statements.quote: p.152: "Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and therefore was most likely a feature of some of the protolanguages as well. ... All the modern languages have at least high and low tone." p.160: "Although tonal contrast is found in virtually all of the the Lakes Plain languages, it will not be shown in the word list transcriptions. Additionally, stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level generalisation only: Lakes Plain languages (Waritai included by scope, as an East Tariku member whose data in this work is a 1986 survey wordlist) are tone languages with at least H and L; stress has not been found contrastive anywhere in the family, and no placement of (non-contrastive) stress is given for Waritai or for the family.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedges: tonal contrast in 'virtually all' Lakes Plain languages; stress non-contrastive 'to date'; only a few original wordlists marked stress at all. Sikaritai (sister East Tariku language) is noted as analysed as pitch-accent by Martin 1991.
new_statements.domain_note: Not a description of Waritai prosody: the statement is a comparative surveyor's summary across the family, resting on published SIL phonologies of other members (Iau, Obokuitai, Doutai, Sikaritai, Edopi, Kirikiri). Waritai-specific material anywhere in print is limited to survey wordlists (McAllister 1986 in Clouse 1997; Voorhoeve 1975 no. 85 'Weretai') with tone and stress unmarked. Word-level (isolated wordlist items); no phrase-level information.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is about the Lakes Plain family as a whole (lake1255), not about Waritai specifically; Waritai (wari1264, = Voorhoeve's 'Weretai' no. 85, village Taiyeve) is covered only by scope. Do not confuse with 'Weirate', a Tause dialect also listed in Clouse 1997, or with the StressTyp Lakes Plain entry, which is Obokuitai (obok1239).

sources.note: Family-level only: p.152 sec. 11 'Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages... All the modern languages have at least high and low tone'; p.160 App. 3: stress not marked in the wordlists because 'it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date'. Waritai itself enters only as a survey wordlist (L. McAllister, April 1986, Taiyeve, p.164) and in segmental remarks on /s/, /p/ and initial clusters (pp.144-146). No statement of stress placement.

sources.citation: Clouse, Helja and Duane Clouse. 1993. Kirikiri and the western Lakes Plains languages: selected phonological phenomena. Language and Linguistics in Melanesia 24: 1-18.
sources.note: Nothing. Waritai appears only on Map 1 and in the classification lists (p.2, population '?'); the paper covers consonants, absence of nasals, constricted high vowels and syllable closure across the western Lakes Plains languages and explicitly leaves 'syllable structure and tone' to future research (Conclusion, p.17). No mention of stress.
